questions.title: Alphabet in a DFA
questions.question: A complete DFA has 4 states and an alphabet of 3 symbols. How many state-symbol entries does δ have?
questions.explanation: There is one entry for each pair in Q×Σ, giving 4×3=12. A drawing may combine several entries into one arrow.

questions.title: Alphabet in a DFA
questions.question: Over Σ={a,b}, how many outgoing symbol choices must be defined at each state?

options.label: It equals the number of final states.

questions.explanation: A complete DFA needs one destination on a and one on b, even if both destinations are the same.

questions.title: Alphabet in a DFA
questions.question: A DFA over {0,1} is to process {0,1,2}. What must be added?

options.label: Nothing; Σ automatically includes every character
A defined transition on 2 from every state
An ε transition from the start

questions.explanation: A larger alphabet expands the domain of δ. The intended behavior on the new symbol must be specified.

questions.title: Alphabet in a DFA
questions.question: When complementing L over Σ, what is the universe?
questions.explanation: Complement means all finite words over the selected alphabet that are not in L, including ε when appropriate.

questions.title: Alphabet in a DFA
questions.question: Let L=a*. What is its complement over Σ={a}?
questions.explanation: a* already contains every word over the unary alphabet. Changing the universe to {a,b}* would change the complement.

questions.title: Alphabet in a DFA
questions.question: Let L=a*. What is its complement over Γ={a,b}?

options.label: All words containing at least one a
All words containing at least one b

questions.explanation: Words made only of a symbols, including ε, are in L. Any b forces a word outside L.

questions.title: Alphabet in a DFA
questions.question: Can two alphabet symbols lead from one state to the same destination in a DFA?

options.label: Only if both symbols are identical.
Only if the destination is rejecting.
Yes; determinism requires one destination per symbol, not different destinations.

questions.explanation: δ may map different arguments to the same state. It is a function, not necessarily an injective function.

questions.title: Alphabet in a DFA
questions.question: A DFA has three states and six drawn arrows; some arrows carry several labels. Can |Σ| be inferred from six alone?

options.label: No; count the individual symbol transitions instead.

questions.explanation: A labeled arrow may represent several δ entries. The equation |Q|×|Σ| counts entries, not graphical arrow objects.

questions.title: Alphabet in a DFA
questions.question: Two automata use alphabets {a} and {a,b}. What should be done before comparing complements over {a,b}?

options.label: Interpret both over {a,b} and specify rejecting behavior on newly added b inputs.
Compare their numbers of states only.

questions.explanation: A common universe is required. Completing the smaller-alphabet recognizer with rejection on b preserves its original language as a subset of the larger universe.

questions.title: Alphabet in a DFA
questions.question: If input contains c but Σ={a,b}, what is formally true?

options.label: c is automatically treated as ε.
c must be accepted because it is a character.
c must loop to the current state.
The input is outside Σ*, so the specified δ does not define its run.

questions.explanation: A recognizer's formal input domain is Σ*. An implementation may report an invalid-symbol error or extend the alphabet with rejecting behavior, but must define that policy.

questions.title: Transition function
questions.question: What is the type of a complete DFA transition function?
questions.explanation: δ returns one next state. The powerset codomain is used for NFAs, and whole-word acceptance is a derived function.

questions.title: Transition function
questions.question: What is δ*(q,ε)?
questions.explanation: Reading no input leaves the current state unchanged. The current state need not be the designated start.

questions.title: Transition function
questions.question: Which recurrence correctly extends δ to words?
questions.explanation: First process the prefix w, then take one transition on the final symbol a. Order generally matters.

questions.title: Transition function
questions.question: Let δ(A,0)=B, δ(A,1)=A, δ(B,0)=A, δ(B,1)=B. What is δ*(A,010)?
questions.explanation: A --0→ B --1→ B --0→ A. Deterministic transitions yield one state.

questions.title: Transition function
questions.question: Using δ(r,0)=2r mod 3 and δ(r,1)=(2r+1) mod 3, what is δ(2,1)?
questions.explanation: 2×2+1=5 and 5 mod 3=2. The destination is the remainder, not the unreduced value.

questions.title: Transition function
questions.question: What condition makes two drawn transitions violate determinism?

options.label: Different sources with the same symbol
Same source and symbol but different destinations

questions.explanation: A function cannot assign two different outputs to one input pair. Sharing labels across different sources is normal.

questions.title: Transition function
questions.question: If a DFA table has a blank destination for (q,a), which statement is accurate?

options.label: It is incomplete unless a destination is supplied by an explicit convention.
It is automatically an accepting transition.

questions.explanation: Under a total δ, every pair requires a value. A blank is not a state or an ε move.

questions.title: Transition function
questions.question: For a parity DFA, δ(E,1)=O and δ(O,1)=E; 0 loops at both states. What is δ*(O,101)?
questions.explanation: Starting at O, the two 1s toggle twice and the 0 leaves parity unchanged: O→E→E→O.

questions.title: Transition function
questions.question: Which information does δ alone omit?

options.label: Whether a given pair maps to q
How a changes the current state

questions.explanation: F is a separate component of the DFA. The same transition graph with different final sets can recognize different languages.

questions.title: Transition function
questions.question: If δ*(p,w)=δ*(q,w), must p and q be equivalent?

options.label: Yes; all states reaching the same state can be merged.
Yes; any common destination proves equivalence.
Only if w is nonempty, then always yes.
No; agreement after one chosen word is insufficient.

questions.explanation: Equivalence requires agreement in acceptance for every suffix, including ε. One common destination does not establish that universal property.

questions.title: NFA
questions.question: What is the codomain of an NFA transition function?
questions.explanation: A transition returns a set of possible destinations, including the empty set. 2^Q means the set of all subsets of Q.

questions.title: NFA
questions.question: What is required for NFA acceptance?

options.label: A path need only visit a final state before input ends.
A majority of paths must accept.
Every path must end in a final state.
At least one complete consuming path can end in a final state.

questions.explanation: Acceptance is existential over complete paths. Rejecting or unfinished alternatives do not cancel an accepting path.

questions.title: NFA
questions.question: Must an NFA have an ε transition?

options.label: No; multiple same-symbol successors alone can make it nondeterministic.
Yes; otherwise it cannot be an NFA.

questions.explanation: ε moves are permitted, not mandatory. A DFA interpreted with singleton destination sets is also an NFA.

questions.title: NFA
questions.question: NFA: start s is nonfinal and loops on 0 and 1; s --1→ f; f is the only final state and has no outgoing edges. What language is recognized?
questions.explanation: An accepting branch chooses the transition to f on the last symbol. If input remains, that branch dies, while the s branch keeps trying.

questions.title: NFA
questions.question: An NFA has nonfinal start s looping on 0 and 1, an extra s --1→ f edge, and only f final with no outgoing edges. Why is 10 rejected?

options.label: A final state automatically rejects its entering symbol.
The branch at f after 1 cannot consume the final 0, and s is nonfinal.

questions.explanation: Reaching f early is not enough. The only surviving state after the whole word is the nonfinal looping state s.

questions.title: NFA
questions.question: Which is guaranteed for every NFA?

options.label: An equivalent DFA with no more states exists.
It has fewer states than every equivalent DFA.

questions.explanation: NFAs and DFAs have the same language power. A DFA may need exponentially more states, and an NFA need not be smaller.

questions.title: NFA
questions.question: To combine disjoint NFAs for R and S into one for R|S, which construction is safe?

options.label: Add a new start with ε edges to both old starts; retain both final sets.
Connect every final of R to S and retain only S finals.
Require both branches to accept the same run.

questions.explanation: The new start chooses either component, implementing union. Connecting R's finals to S's start implements concatenation instead.

questions.title: NFA
questions.question: For disjoint NFAs recognizing R and S, how is concatenation RS constructed?

options.label: Link R finals to S start by ε and make only S finals accepting.
Keep all R finals accepting without qualification.
Link both starts to a new start by ordinary a edges.

questions.explanation: A successful run must finish an R word and then an S word. Retaining R finals can wrongly accept an R word without the S portion when ε∉S.

questions.title: NFA
questions.question: For a safe star construction on an arbitrary NFA, why use a fresh accepting start?

options.label: It admits zero repetitions without treating a return to the old start as a completed factor.
It requires the original language to contain ε.
It removes the need to consume symbols.

questions.explanation: Add ε from the new start to the old start, and from old finals back to the old start and to a new final as needed. Reusing an old start with incoming edges can admit incomplete factors.

questions.title: NFA
questions.question: If every NFA branch dies before consuming all input, what is the result?

options.label: Acceptance if one branch once visited a final state

questions.explanation: No complete accepting path exists. A dead branch cannot ignore the unread suffix.

questions.title: Nondeterminism
questions.question: Does NFA acceptance depend on a random branch being lucky?

options.label: No; it asks whether any accepting path exists.
Yes; acceptance means probability above one half.
Yes; each run accepts with a probability.
Only when ε edges are used.

questions.explanation: Nondeterminism defines existence, not a randomized algorithm. A simulator must preserve all relevant possibilities.

questions.title: Nondeterminism
questions.question: One complete path accepts and 99 complete paths reject. What does the NFA do?

options.label: Accept with probability 1/100 as its formal result

questions.explanation: One witness path suffices. The number of rejecting alternatives does not affect language membership.

questions.title: Nondeterminism
questions.question: No complete path accepts, but one reaches a final state with unread input. What happens?

options.label: Accept only if the unread part repeats

questions.explanation: The full input must be consumed. An early final state does not satisfy acceptance for the longer word.

questions.title: Nondeterminism
questions.question: Which simulation strategy is correct in general?

options.label: Update the entire set of possible states at each input position.
Choose the shortest path and stop at its first final state.
Choose the first outgoing edge and discard the others.

questions.explanation: Set simulation retains every path's possible current state. Greedy selection can lose the only accepting path.

questions.title: Nondeterminism
questions.question: Why can an NFA for an ending pattern be compact?

options.label: It can store an unbounded integer in one state.
It can keep scanning while also trying candidate starts of the final pattern.
It can read the input backward for free.

questions.explanation: Branching lets the machine guess where the final pattern begins while another branch continues scanning. It does not add unbounded memory.

questions.title: Nondeterminism
questions.question: If an NFA has only one successor per symbol and no ε moves but some missing transitions, what is it?

options.label: A deterministic partial transition structure, valid as an NFA
A machine that accepts all missing inputs
A complete DFA under the course definition

questions.explanation: It has no branching, but completeness is missing for a formal DFA. Adding a rejecting sink completes it.

questions.title: Nondeterminism
questions.question: For a union construction, what does choosing either component mean?

options.label: Each branch must consume a different word.
The same whole input is tested by one branch or the other.
Half the input goes to each branch automatically.

questions.explanation: Union tests membership in at least one language. Splitting the word into consecutive parts is concatenation, not union.

questions.title: Nondeterminism
questions.question: Can two distinct paths merge into the same state at the same input position?

options.label: Yes, but the word must then be accepted.
No; path identity must be stored forever.
Only if they used no symbols.
Yes; keeping one copy of that state preserves future acceptance possibilities.

questions.explanation: Future behavior depends on state and remaining input, not the history of how the state was reached.

questions.title: Nondeterminism
questions.question: Which property makes subset simulation finite even when ε cycles exist?

options.label: It bans ε from regular expressions.
It records visited states, so repeated visits add no new state.
It treats every cycle as acceptance.

questions.explanation: ε-closure is reachability in a finite graph. Repeating a state does not require a new configuration at the same input position.

questions.title: Nondeterminism
questions.question: If one NFA has more paths than another, must it recognize more words?

options.label: Yes; each path contributes a distinct word.
Only if their alphabets agree, then yes.
No; extra paths may accept no new word.
Yes; all loops add ε to the language.

questions.explanation: Multiple paths can spell the same word, or be nonaccepting. Languages record words rather than path counts.

questions.title: Multiple successor states
questions.question: If δ(q,a)={r,s}, how many input symbols are consumed on either branch?

options.label: One symbol on r and zero on s

questions.explanation: Both possible transitions are labeled a. Each alternative consumes the same one input symbol.

questions.title: Multiple successor states
questions.question: Let δ(p,a)={p,r} and δ(q,a)={r,s}. From {p,q}, what is the successor set before ε-closure?
questions.explanation: Take the union of destination sets. Do not intersect them, keep a set of sets, or retain q merely because it was previously active.

questions.title: Multiple successor states
questions.question: What does δ(q,a)=∅ mean in an NFA?

options.label: The whole NFA must reject every word.
No path from q can consume a.

questions.explanation: The branch at q dies on a. Other simultaneously active states may still have valid a transitions.

questions.title: Multiple successor states
questions.question: NFA: δ(s,0)={s,t}, δ(t,0)={u}; no ε edges. Starting at s, what states are possible after 00?
questions.explanation: After the first 0 the set is {s,t}; the second produces {s,t} from s and {u} from t.

questions.title: Multiple successor states
questions.question: NFA with start s: δ(s,0)={s,t}, δ(t,0)={u}, δ(u,0)=∅; there are no ε edges and only u is final. Is 00 accepted?

options.label: No; every active state must be final.
Yes; u is possible after the whole word.
Yes; because all paths end at u.
No; s is also possible and nonfinal.

questions.explanation: Acceptance requires at least one final state in the reached set. Here other nonfinal possibilities do not matter.

questions.title: Multiple successor states
questions.question: Suppose the current set is {p,q}, δ(p,b)=∅ and δ(q,b)={r}. What happens on b?

options.label: The new set before closure is {r}.

questions.explanation: Only the p branch disappears. The q branch consumes b and survives at r.

questions.title: Multiple successor states
questions.question: If two edges from q on a both lead to r, how many copies of r are stored in δ(q,a)?
questions.explanation: Transition results are sets. Duplicate identical edges do not change the recognized language.

questions.title: Multiple successor states
questions.question: If S contains five NFA states and each has two a-successors, how many distinct successors are possible at most before ε-closure?
questions.explanation: The union has at most ten entries before deduplication and cannot exceed the entire NFA state set.

questions.title: Multiple successor states
questions.question: Which rule correctly tests whether an active subset S is accepting?
questions.explanation: At least one active state must be final. The other conditions are either too strong or wrong for empty sets.

questions.title: Multiple successor states
questions.question: From the empty active set ∅, what is the successor on any symbol?
questions.explanation: The union over no active states is empty, and ε-closure of the empty set is empty. No branch restarts automatically.

questions.title: Epsilon transitions
questions.question: What does an ε transition consume?
questions.explanation: ε means the empty word, not whitespace or a wildcard.

questions.title: Epsilon transitions
questions.question: Does ε-closure({q}) contain q if q has no ε edges?

options.label: No; at least one move is required.
Only if q is the start.

questions.explanation: Reachability by zero or more ε moves includes the starting state itself.

questions.title: Epsilon transitions
questions.question: Given p --ε→ q --ε→ r and no other ε edges, what is ε-closure({p})?
questions.explanation: Follow the full chain and include p. Looking only one edge ahead misses r.

questions.title: Epsilon transitions
questions.question: Given p --ε→ q and q --a→ r, what is ε-closure({p})?
questions.explanation: Closure follows ε edges only. Reaching r requires consuming a.

questions.title: Epsilon transitions
questions.question: If q0 is nonfinal but ε-closure({q0}) contains a final state, is ε accepted?

options.label: Only if all closure states are final
No; q0 must itself be final in every NFA

questions.explanation: An NFA can reach a final state without consuming input. The DFA criterion q0∈F is a special case with no ε moves.

questions.title: Epsilon transitions
questions.question: Given p --ε→ q and q --ε→ p, does computing closure require infinitely many stored states?

options.label: Yes; each loop creates a fresh state.

questions.explanation: Repeated graph visits do not create new states. Track visited states to terminate.

questions.title: Epsilon transitions
questions.question: An NFA takes a --symbol transition into r, then r --ε→ f with f final. Can this help acceptance after the last input symbol?

options.label: Only if a is the empty word.
Only if r is also final.
Yes; ε moves may occur after input is consumed.
No; all ε moves must precede the first symbol.

questions.explanation: Acceptance allows a path whose consumed labels form exactly the input, including trailing ε edges.

questions.title: Epsilon transitions
questions.question: Which identity is true for ε-closure E?
questions.explanation: Once every ε-reachable state is included, applying closure again adds nothing. Closure is independent of final status.

questions.title: Epsilon transitions
questions.question: How is ε-closure of a set S obtained?

options.label: Intersect the ε-closures of its member states.
Union the ε-closures of its member states.
Add every state with an incoming symbol edge.
Keep only the first state's closure.

questions.explanation: A state is reachable from S if reachable from any member. This gives a union.

questions.title: Epsilon transitions
questions.question: Which is the correct NFA update for an ε-closed active set S on a?
questions.explanation: Consume one a from every currently possible state, combine destinations, then include all ε continuations.

questions.title: Scanner or lexer
questions.question: What is the primary input/output transformation of a scanner?

options.label: Source program to proof of correctness

questions.explanation: Lexical analysis groups characters into tokens. Parsing and code generation are later compiler responsibilities.

questions.title: Scanner or lexer
questions.question: Which pair names the same compiler stage here?
questions.explanation: Scanner and lexer are synonyms for the lexical-analysis component.

questions.title: Scanner or lexer
questions.question: Which task belongs primarily to a parser rather than a basic scanner?

options.label: Checking how tokens fit the language's grammar
Skipping a comment under the lexical rules
Recognizing a run of digits as an integer token

questions.explanation: Grammar operates on token structure. The other tasks are lexical.

questions.title: Scanner or lexer
questions.question: With tokens ID=[a-z]+, INT=[0-9]+ and PLUS='+', which input contains a lexical error if spaces are skipped?
questions.explanation: @ matches no declared token. x 2 may later be a syntax error, but both lexemes can still be tokenized.

questions.title: Scanner or lexer
questions.question: Does successful tokenization guarantee a syntactically correct program?

options.label: Yes; DFAs check every grammar rule.
No; valid tokens can appear in an invalid order.
Only if the scanner is generated.

questions.explanation: For example, valid operator and operand tokens may still form a malformed expression. Parser and semantic checks remain separate.

questions.title: Scanner or lexer
questions.question: What is complete-pass scanning?

options.label: Produce the entire token stream before returning it.
Accept only if every DFA state is final.
Produce exactly one token per source character.

questions.explanation: Complete-pass and iterative scanning describe output scheduling, not different token languages.

questions.title: Scanner or lexer
questions.question: What is iterative scanning?

options.label: Repeat a token until a parser accepts it.
Reread the whole file once per token type.
Return the next token when requested.

questions.explanation: A parser can request tokens one at a time while the scanner retains its input position.

questions.title: Scanner or lexer
questions.question: When may a scanner safely discard whitespace?

options.label: When the language's lexical rules declare that whitespace insignificant at that position.
Only when whitespace is not in the character alphabet.

questions.explanation: Spaces inside a string can be part of its value, and some languages give indentation meaning. The course examples simplify this policy.

questions.title: Scanner or lexer
questions.question: Why does a scanner need more than a bare yes/no DFA recognizer?

options.label: Scanners must recognize nonregular token patterns.
A DFA can recognize only one-word languages.
It must identify token boundaries and types and often return values.

questions.explanation: The automaton supports recognition, while scanner logic handles repeated tokens, outputs, errors, and selection policies.

questions.title: Scanner or lexer
questions.question: Which statement about comments is correct?

options.label: They can be removed without considering string-literal boundaries.
They are always passed unchanged to the parser.
They can be recognized and skipped while still affecting source position tracking.
Every slash begins a comment in every language.

questions.explanation: A scanner follows the specified comment and string rules. Skipping a comment does not remove the need to maintain line/column locations.

questions.title: Token and token stream
questions.question: For (IDENTIFIER,"myVar"), which is the token type?
questions.explanation: The type classifies the lexeme; the value or spelling carries its particular content.

questions.title: Token and token stream
questions.question: What is a token stream?

options.label: An unordered set of token types

questions.explanation: Order matters for parsing. Repeated tokens remain repeated sequence elements.

questions.title: Token and token stream
questions.question: With ID=[a-z][a-z0-9]* and INT=[0-9]+, how is abc42 tokenized by maximal munch?

options.label: One ID token with lexeme abc42
A lexical error because digits occur

questions.explanation: The entire five-character lexeme matches ID, so it beats the shorter accepted prefix abc.

questions.title: Token and token stream
questions.question: With operators '=' and '==', what is the first token in === under longest-match scanning?
questions.explanation: The longest declared operator prefix is two characters. A subsequent '=' token remains.

questions.title: Token and token stream
questions.question: Rules include keyword if and ID=[a-z]+. With longest match first and keyword priority on ties, how is ifx tokenized?

options.label: KW_IF followed by a lexical error

questions.explanation: The three-character ID is longer than the two-character keyword. Tie priority does not override a longer match.
